name: Ciclopirox shampoo

lead: Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated antifungal wash used to clear the flaking, redness and itching of seborrheic dermatitis, the inflamed scalp condition that overlaps with dandruff. The payoff is a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. It is prescription-only in the US.

Ciclopirox is a hydroxypyridone antifungal active against Malassezia yeasts and described as having anti-inflammatory properties; its mechanism differs from the azoles and is not fully understood. Randomized trials have tested the 1% shampoo against vehicle for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and as an adjunct in childhood tinea capitis. No trial found tested it for hair growth.

paras: People use it as a regular medicated wash, often alternating with or alongside ketoconazole shampoo in hair-loss and scalp-care circles. Flaking typically improves over a few weeks of repeated use.
Systemic absorption from topical use is reported to be low. It is a prescription medicine in the US and Canada; local irritation is the usual concern with medicated shampoos.

angle.text: Ciclopirox shampoo targets the Malassezia yeast behind scalp flaking and redness, leaving a cleaner, flake-free scalp and hair. Several vehicle-controlled trials cover seborrheic dermatitis; none have examined hair growth.

lead: Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated shampoo built around ciclopirox, a synthetic hydroxypyridone antifungal with reported anti-inflammatory properties. It is used mainly for seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, the flaking, redness and itching condition that overlaps with ordinary dandruff.[1][2] For appearance, the payoff is a calmer, clearer scalp: less visible flaking on the scalp and shoulders, less redness along the hairline, and less itch-driven scratching.[2][3]

Ciclopirox is active against Malassezia yeasts, which are widely thought to take part in seborrheic dermatitis, and the shampoo has been tested in several large randomized trials.[2][3][4] Wikipedia notes that a 2007 comparison found efficacy similar to ketoconazole shampoo, with some added symptom relief that may reflect its anti-inflammatory action.[1] Seborrheic dermatitis can sometimes be accompanied by temporary shedding or thinning when the scalp is inflamed, so people in hair communities sometimes treat scalp flaking and inflammation as part of keeping the scalp in good condition.[5]

In hair-loss and grooming communities ciclopirox shampoo is a minor topic next to ketoconazole shampoo, and it comes up as a prescription antifungal alternative or companion. Published trials have examined it for seborrheic dermatitis and, as an adjunct, for tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) in children; none found tested it as a hair-growth treatment.[6][7] In the United States it is prescription-only.[1]
infobox: Topical (shampoo; also nail lacquer and creams)
Prescription-only in the US and Canada; pharmacy medicine (S2) in Australia[1]

paras: The best-documented use is seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, which shows up as scaling, redness and itching, often in a band along the hairline and behind the ears. Wikipedia describes the condition as affecting roughly 1 to 5 percent of the general population, tending to be chronic with periods of relapse, and with scalp involvement that can resemble dandruff.[5] Ciclopirox 1% shampoo has been the subject of several randomized trials in this condition.[2][3][8]

A 2007 comparison cited by Wikipedia described ciclopirox as an alternative to ketoconazole with similar efficacy and greater subjective symptom relief, possibly because of its anti-inflammatory action.[1] Wikipedia's article on seborrheic dermatitis lists ketoconazole and ciclopirox among the antifungal shampoos with the strongest evidence, alongside selenium disulfide, zinc pyrithione and piroctone olamine.[5]

Ciclopirox shampoo has also been studied as an adjunct to oral griseofulvin in children with tinea capitis.[6][7] Other ciclopirox formulations, such as the 8 percent nail lacquer, are used for mild to moderate fungal nail infections.[1]

Wikipedia describes the mechanism of ciclopirox as poorly understood and distinct from the azole antifungals; a 2003 yeast study suggested effects on DNA repair, cell division and intracellular transport, and loss of function of certain catalase and peroxidase enzymes has been implicated.[1] Reviews describe it as effective in vitro and in vivo against Malassezia yeasts and as having anti-inflammatory properties; an Italian trial report adds antibacterial and antioxidant properties to that list.[4][8]
With prolonged topical use, systemic absorption is reported as under 5 percent, with protein binding of 94 to 97 percent and an elimination half-life of about 1.7 hours.[1]

A US trial enrolled 499 patients with scalp seborrheic dermatitis who applied ciclopirox 1% shampoo or vehicle twice weekly for four weeks. Effective treatment, defined as scores of 0 or 1 for disease status, scaling and erythema, was reached in 26.0 percent of the ciclopirox group and 12.9 percent of the vehicle group. Most adverse events were mild, mostly skin reactions, at similar rates in both groups.[2]

A European multicenter trial across 45 centers in Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Austria randomized 949 patients to ciclopirox once or twice weekly or vehicle for four weeks. Response rates were 57.9 percent with twice-weekly use and 45.4 percent with once-weekly use, against 31.6 percent for vehicle. Responders then entered a 12-week prophylaxis phase in which relapse rates were compared between ciclopirox regimens and vehicle.[3]

A 203-patient trial compared vehicle with ciclopirox 0.1%, 0.3% and 1% shampoos applied twice weekly for four weeks. All ciclopirox groups trended toward improvement, with the largest change in the 1% group, whose sum score fell from 8.3 to 4.4 (P = 0.0372 versus vehicle).[9] An assessor-blinded Italian trial in moderate-to-severe scalp seborrheic dermatitis was published in 2019.[8] Narrative reviews summarize the body of work and describe the shampoo as effective and well tolerated.[4][10]

In tinea capitis, a randomized double-blind study of 40 children compared selenium sulfide 1% and ciclopirox 1% shampoos twice weekly as adjuncts to eight weeks of ultramicronized griseofulvin. By week 8, 30 of 33 evaluable children (90.9 percent) had mycological cure, and the two shampoos were equally effective as adjuncts.[6] A registered trial of selenium sulfide, ketoconazole and ciclopirox shampoos as additional treatments for scalp ringworm enrolled 47 participants.[7]
No published trials found test ciclopirox shampoo for hair growth in androgenetic alopecia.

Ciclopirox shampoo is a small topic compared with ketoconazole shampoo in hair-loss communities. Where it appears, participants discuss it as a prescription antifungal option for scalp inflammation and dandruff-type flaking, sometimes as a rotation partner with other medicated shampoos. Legal status varies by country: prescription-only in the US and Canada, and a Schedule 2 pharmacy medicine in Australia.[1] In 2023 ciclopirox was reported as the 278th most commonly prescribed medication in the US, across all its formulations.[1]
